entries.translation: (1) Nzaikonini (small circumcision at age 4–5 by operator Mwaiki, dressed with Undu & Kithanzi; knife-wetting taboo = Mundu wa wenzi / Mundu wa mwa) • (2) Nzaikoneni (great initiation under tutor Mubwiki: Wa-Singi shoot Telembo lizards, sham cattle raid pelting Ngñondu fruit, Mumbo fig sap sealed with Ndumunya iron nail, and Kulu Kilwa cattle gift) • 9 Pictographic Riddles (Ndeto) on the Musai Stick (Mthiwa wood, pp. 71–72): 1. Kithembo (wooden honey jar) • (3) Mbabani (Kitui/Kibwezi men's secret bush initiation with roaring tube, Ngima ya Mbabani, Ngai wands, and sand arrow pass-sign ↑ → ≁) & Choo Muumba (Mumoni Tana river beast rite)

entries.english: Traditional Kamba Folktale Genre (Wano), 6 Classic Tales & 4 Aiimu Legends Recorded by C. W. Hobley (1910 pp. 86–92, 107–117)
entries.translation: 6 Verbatim Wano Tales (Ch. XXI, pp. 107–117): (1) Origin of Death (Engai sends frog Chua, chameleon Kimbu calling 'Niwe, niwe, niwe', and thrush Itoroko / Siotoroka who wakes at 2 a.m.), (2) The Hyaena (Mbiti posing as suitor Mutili and biting off his mother-in-law's sheep's fat tail), (3) How the Animals Got Their Marks (medicine man painting leopard Ngo, hyaena Mbiti, hartebeest Gondi, and zebra Njai after testing their singing), (4) The Hare (Wa-paruku / Buku) & the Lion (Mutwa Ubiu — burying tails crying 'Nthi Nthi Kumeseo' and jumping the 'tule Kithito' peace fire), (5) The Tortoise (Ngu) & the Fish Eagle (Kipalala — racing to the coast for sea salt with relays answering 'Ngu iko? — Ni iko'), (6) The Cunning of the Hare & Rainmaker Munei's Prophecy at Mbuanii • Aiimu Legends (Ch. entries.english: Kamba Salutations, 5 Verbatim Riddles (Kweta ndai), Dances, Musical Instruments (Mbebe) & Star Lore in Hobley (1910 pp. 32–33, 52–56)
entries.translation: Salutations (p. 52): Man/Woman or Elder/Elder: Umuvoo! → Inimuvoo! | Young man (Anake) to young man: Waiya! → Waiya! | Man to child: Nosio! → Ah! | Man to youth: Oponiao! → Ah! | Man to girl (Muitu): Wakia! → Ah! • 5 Riddles (Kweta ndai, p. 54): (1) Nduma ('What fastens up the moon?') → Muumbi (Clouds); (2) O-Selia ('What first goes forward and then back?') → Kimbu (Chameleon); (3) Mwetu etiki ('My mother is very big') → Kulotoi (Wild banana); (4) Tuna Kwatana ('We take hold of each other') → Nzia na nzia (Crossroads); (5) Wo wiwa ('The heart likes it') → Kinto Kitheo (A pleasant thing) • Songs & Dances (p. 53): Mavio & Kwina wathi wa Mavio (wedding), Kuia Muntu (funeral), Kilumi (women's harvest/birth trance dance), Wathi (youth dance), Kuthia & Kuisia chubi (tilling songs), Cheli (Mumoni dance) • Musical Instruments (pp. 32–33): Mbebe (bowed 1-stringed gourd fiddle), Soo (bamboo/gourd bugle or eland/kudu horn), Nguli / Zomali (hill-top warning whistle), Kithembi, Ngutha, Engoma & 4-ft ground-beaten Muvungu / Cha drums • Star Lore & Game (pp. 54–56): Wa-Isa (star-people whose bathing brings rain; meteor = Mu-Isa visiting earth), Kithioi (morning star), Ngenyandi (evening star), Ndata mulili (comet), Utahathi (rainbow), Mutingwano (1-row 10-hole bau game)

entries.english: Social Grades, Kinship Tree, 19 Crops, Weapons (Moluka/Maange/Musi), Law, 3 Ordeals, Kithito & Kingñoli in Hobley (1910)
entries.translation: Social Grades (p. 49): Kivisi (pl. Nisi, boy) → Mwanake (pl. Anake, warrior) → Nthele (pl. Anthele, married man) → Mutumia / Mutumia munene wa muthanga (elder / territorial chief); Muitu (pl. Weitu, girl) → Mundu mukaa (unmarried woman) → Kipeti (pl. Ipeti, mother) → Mukuu (old woman; Ngungu childless woman) • Kinship (p. 50): Asa (father), Mweitu (mother), Mundu asa / Umaa (paternal/maternal grandfather), Susu (grandmother), Mwanaya (brother / brother- or sister-in-law), Ukulu (elder sister), Mweitu aya (younger sister), Mukaa akaa (my wife), Mwe mewa (my husband), Muthonua (mother-/son-in-law), Njugulu akwa (grandchild) • Food, 19 Crops & Crafts (pp. 15–33): Usuru (gruel stirred with Mui), Kitheki (milk-gruel), Ngima (porridge), Lungñuyu & Koho (aromatic herbs), Ukiya-iwa (sugar-cane beer fermented with Miatini sausage-tree fruit, drunk on Thomi clearing from Njeli/Kiku gourds), Uwindi & Kika firesticks, Mwatu beehive & Kithembi wa Uki honey drum, 4 traps (Mukwa, Ikehengi, Mwito, Kisungula) • Weapons & War (pp. 43–48): 3 arrows (Moluka unfeathered, Maange hardwood, Musi iron-tipped with Ivai strophanthus/scorpion poison), Ubiu sword & Nzomo elder's sword, Ndata club, Ngwalo finger-strips of a Mutwe tumo / Mutwe ubiu • Law, Ordeals & Religion (pp. 47–48, 78–106, 167–168): Grave Offence customary restitution (Ulu 11 cows + 1 bull; Kitui 13 cows + 1 bull), Kithito peace & judicial oath (insulated on 3 stones, hidden in Ngunga rocks), 3 Ordeals (red-hot Ubiu sword, spurt-gourd water ordeal, tear-duct bead ordeal), Kingñoli collective execution after 7 witchcraft victims, Ukuu purification with Ngñondu, Mundu mue (white magic, Kititi cha Mbuu divining gourd with Muthiwa ferrule & Mbui bell, Iga white clay) vs. Muoiin (black magic), Engai / Mulungu & Aiimu (plus Aiimu ya Kitombo & spiritual husbands of married women)

entries.translation: 4 Population Centres: Ulu / Yulu ('up there', west of Athi river, speaking kīkamba kīluŋgalu 'real Kikamba'; SW Kilungu people call other Ulu Akamba æβau; Anoka hunter-gatherers on Mt. Noka), Kitui District (east of Athi & Yata plateau, called aþaisu / kīþaisu by Ulu; cattle-owning ŋgoβə vs. beehive-climbing īkuli 'baboons'), Mumoni (north, retaining r), and Kikumbuliu (south-east) • Kamba Names for Neighbours (pp. 9–22, 573): Swahili = asumba (archaic maþomba 'burden-bearers'; Mombasa Swahili call Akamba Warimangao / Waumanguo 'those who go naked'), Giriama = aswī (language kīswī, country uswīnī), Taita = andī (from ndī baobab strings), Duruma = aluluma, Mbere = ambele, Tharaka = aþaka, Kikuyu = akīkuyu, Maasai = akaβi (archaic akīþoŋgo from Kisongo SE of Kilimanjaro), Oromo/Galla = atwa (country utwa), Somali = aŋgoloŋgo, Nubians = anoβi, Europeans = asuŋgu / andu atunə ('red people', p. 560), Rabai 1836 famine emigrants = atumwa / maðīkīlambua ('rain-followers') • Tanganyika / German East Africa Enclaves (pp. 569–573): Upare, Usambara (Buiti, Kalamera, Gonya), Uguru (Kerenge, Gedja), Usagara (Mangubugubu), Useguha, Uluguru, Usaramo (Mkamba, Bagamoyo, Saadani), plus Chagga (Wadjagga) ruling clans in Useri, Mkuu, Kenj, Mwika, Marangu (Chief Mareale from Umon/Mumoni; 2nd chief Ngovi) & Oru (Wamaturu, Wandzau < nzau 'bull')

entries.english: Childbirth, Infancy, 4th-Day Īþa Neck-Chain & Birth Anomalies (Lindblom 1920 Ch. II, pp. 29–41 & Ch. XXXV, pp. 562–563)
entries.translation: Umbilical cord = mukautī (cut with iron knife in West Ukamba, sharpened sugarcane stem in East Ukamba); placenta = nžuu / ŋgua īa kana ('child's dress', buried outside hut); premature baby = muīnde (wrapped in warm sheepskin near hearth); 3-stone water-fetching rite with kīumo fig twig & īkoka grass; utindīti & ŋgīma Eleusine porridge thrown over the hut roof to children; 4th-day iron neck-chain = īþa (hung on the baby's neck after parental ritual coitus to transform the infant from a kīīmu spirit-child into a human being); turning the child on the mother's left arm = olula kana • Birth Anomalies (pp. 37–38, 562–563): breech birth = mundu wa kīu / mundu wa muuo; caul birth = ŋgunīkīlī (can only marry another caul-born person); child cutting upper teeth first = mundu wa kīumīlo / mundu wa kīluli (cannot take the first bite of meat, drink milk first, or eat bananas from an old plantation without ritual); twins = maβaþa (one exposed in past or second given to a friend after mundu muə purification); child born with a 6th finger or toe (polydactyly) = ndula; toeing-in runner = ndaŋgi / matæŋgo; cross-eyed / one-eyed person = nžoŋgo; blind person = kīlīnda; baby-carrier skin = ŋgoī

entries.english: The Three Nžaīko Initiation Degrees: Kaβīu, Mbusīa (Great Rhinoceros Rite) & Mbæβanī (Men's Secret Rite) (Lindblom 1920 Ch. III, pp. 42–71)
entries.translation: (1) 1st Degree — nžaīko īla nīnī / nžaīko īa kaβīu / nžaīko īekondə (physical circumcision by mwaīkī, boys foreskin, girls clitoris uþuþu / mother's euphemism ukaþi; fee 1 bull = mbuī sīa nžaīko, 3-day seclusion drinking unfermented sugarcane juice mutulī; wetting the knife = mundu wa mwa) • (2) 2nd Degree — nžaīko īla nænə / nžaīko īa mbusīa / nžaīko īa muīeh ('Great Circumcision of the Rhinoceros' in the sacred hut īþunu / kīeŋgo kīa nžaīko / īlwanda): novices = asīŋgī (sg. musīŋgī), instructors = aβwīkī (sg. muβwīkī) performing kuta, song-leader = ŋguī; Day 1: 5 obstacles (madīŋgo) & sugarcane arches; Day 2: 'shooting the rhinoceros' (kwaþa mbusīa, roaring made by blowing a mwaeþa reed pipe into a pot of beer and water); Day 3: miniature bow & mwaŋgī bird-arrows; Day 4: interpreting carved pictographic sticks (musaī / ukaī, Figs. 1–8) & sand-drawings (Figs. 9–16); Day 5: sacred mumbu fig-tree sap (wumbu) & glans incision (muβwa); Day 7: sham Maasai raid with ndoŋgu Solanum fruits & sword-tapping on elders' stools • (3) 3rd Degree — nžaīko īa aumə / mbæβanī / mbaβanī ('Circumcision of the Men' held every 3–4 years in Eastern Ukamba to become a mundu wa ŋguma): V-shaped kīusīa bull-roarer pipes (mbæβanī), 4 rank-fires (asīŋgī, ŋgala, aβwīkī, nžama), pulling out a ground-peg with the teeth while squatting over a mock pit, running the gauntlet of ŋgala switches, 5 secret recognition signs (p. 67), and final head-shaving (nīænzīə asīŋgī) marking rebirth (kusīawa)

entries.english: Marriage Customs, Bride-Price (Kwasīa), Nðonī In-Law Avoidance, Kwīua Name-Taboo & Women's Register (Lindblom 1920 Chs. IV–V & Addenda, pp. 72–98, 574)
entries.translation: Bride-Price & Wedding (kwasīa / kuþoa mwīītu, pp. 72–88): 2 proposal goats (mbuī sīa nðeo), beer transport (kuβīkīla ukī), ceremonial offering buck (ndæŋgə īa kwītīa mbuī nðakamə nðī), beer for washing calabashes (wa uþambīa nžeelə), plus 2 cows, 2 bulls/oxen & 40–100 goats recorded on a notched tally-stick (kīka kīa kutala mbuī); maternal family food visits = kuþoka (source of personal name Nðoki); mock bride-capture & weeping songs = mbaþī sīa maīīo; widow = muka wa ndīwa; hospitality custom = kuðīta • Nðonī Avoidance (pp. 89–98): between a man and his mother-in-law (muþonī / muþonwa); reconciled by 'buying fire' (þoa mwakī) and 'killing nðonī' (ua nðonī, Kisese anecdote p. 91) or ua ŋgeanī ('kill mutual refusal', p. 93) • 14 Kwīua Name-Taboo Substitutions (pp. 93–94): kīoko ('tomorrow') → uī; kīlonžo ('noise') → ŋguaīa; īlondu ('sheep') → ŋgondu; nžukī ('bee') → ndoŋgoŋgi; nžoka ('snake') → nīamu īa nðī / īkīlu; wa mbua ('of rain') → nduþu; ŋgomo ('adze/chisel') → ndæβo; mbesa ('pice') → īβulī ('ear-ring'); nzau ('white') → ndeuβu; þomə ('kraal yard') → īβuβeonī / muumaloni; mwatū ('beehive') → mwaŋgo; ītwīku ('ravine') → wīnuka; mwæī ('moon') → musesīa nðī ('that which makes the earth gleam') • 7 Exclusive Women's Words (Addenda p. 574): mbunu ('castor-oil seeds', for mbaīkī), kīowu ('water', for manžī), kīsīeelī ('wind', for ŋgutanī), kwīsonoka ('to be ashamed', for kwīwīa nðonī), īma / īsuma mīno ('sheep', for īlondu), mbuβaŋga ('firewood', old women's word for ŋgu), ukaþi ('horn' → euphemism for uncircumcised girl's clitoris uþuþu)

entries.english: Age-Grades (Īika / Ndukə) & 6 Kukula Meat-Eating Ranks of the Atumīa Elders (Lindblom 1920 Ch. IX, pp. 142–148)
entries.translation: Life Stages (pp. 142–143): kana (infant) → kaβīsi / kīβīsi (uncircumcised/herding boy) & kælætū / mwīītu (girl) → mwanakə (circumcised warrior dancing and raiding) → nðælə (young married man) & kīβætī (married mother) → mutumīa (elder carrying the 3-legged stool mumbə) → atumīa ma kīsuka (executive club/police elders) → atumīa ma nžama / atumīa ma īþæmbo (supreme council & shrine elders carrying the forked staff maka; their wives become īβætī sīa īþæmbo / īβætī sīa nžama via the mboka banana feast, p. 221) • 6 Kukula / Kukusa Meat-Eating Promotion Grades (pp. 144–145): (1) Fee of 1 goat → mutumīa wa mutwə (right to eat goat's head), (2) 1st bull → lower leg of cattle, (3) 2nd bull → upper leg, (4) 3rd bull → loins & brisket, (5) 4th bull → cattle hump (kīaə), (6) 5th bull → cattle tongue & head (full nžama rank)

entries.english: Akamba Law (Nðkwanī), Customary Restitution Schedules, Kīþītū vs. Ndundu Oaths, 6 Ordeals, Kīŋgolə & Curses (Lindblom 1920 Ch. XI, pp. 152–185)
entries.translation: Lawsuit & Customary Restitution (pp. 152–165): lawsuit = nðkwanī ('the case drank water' nðkwanī yanīwa manžī when settled); customary restitution customary restitution: 11 cows + 1 bull in Ulu (1st cow from killer's herd = ŋgombə īa wīumo; 11th cow for victim's widow = ŋgombə īa ndulota 'cow of the broken bow', plus a 12th human victim from the aæī clan in past; half for accidental killing mbaŋga) vs. 13 cows + 1 bull in Kitui; woman's life = 4–5 cows + 1 bull in Ulu (7 + 1 in Kitui); injury tariff (1 finger = 1 goat–1 bull; 2 fingers = 1 bull; 1 eye = 1 bull + 1 goat; 1 arm = 1 cow + 1 bull; 1 leg = 5 cows; both legs = 8 cows); fence-goat = mbuī īa maþanzū; outcast disowned by family = mukoə ('spit/saliva') • Kīþītū vs. Ndundu Oath (pp. 165–173): kuna / kuīa kīþītū ('strike/eat kīþītū' placed on 3 stones while swearer stands naked on 7 stones and strikes it thrice with a mukulwa Acalypha twig); in intra-clan/family cases where kīþītū would kill the whole clan, elders administer ndundu (tips of a bull's heart & tongue, neck-bone ŋgata, and blood in the gall-bladder laid on mwea acacia branches and pierced with a thorn) so only the perjurer dies • 6 Judicial Ordeals (pp. 173–176): (A) kīþītū kīa kīβīu (licking red-hot knife smeared with medicine), (B) red-hot needle through lower lip, (C) kīuma (2 china beads blown into suspect's eyes), (D) ŋgunīko (wax-plugged water calabash spurting water on the thief), (E) mboŋgolo bark poison drink, (F) jumping over fire • Lynch-Law Kīŋgolə (pp. 176–180): shooting recidivist sorcerers (`mwoī`) or thieves after family consent • Women's Collective Justice (īβætī sīī na ŋgolano beating kīþæmbə drums, pp. 180–182, 275) • 4 Curses (Kīumo) & Father's Spittle Blessing (Kīaþīmo, pp. 182–185)

entries.english: Traditional Warfare (Īta), 3 Tactical Divisions, War-Flute (Ŋgulī) & 6 Trophy Titles (Matuso) (Lindblom 1920 Ch. XII, pp. 186–205)
entries.translation: Commanders = asīlīlī (sg. musīlīlī); scouts = aþīanī (carrying protective night-jar medicine mbawa, p. 578); war-flute of Thomson's gazelle horn = ŋgulī (blowing tonal warning signals: aka-βi, aka-βi, mæ-kuka 'The Maasai are coming!', Fig. 53, p. 192); warrior's zebra-mane chest frame = wea (Fig. 54, p. 194) • 3 Tactical Divisions in Attacking a Maasai Kraal (mbīlī, p. 193): (1) muena (picked archers surrounding the el-moran warrior kraal), (2) ŋgīla (warriors seizing cattle inside the enclosure), (3) īta (main body driving off cattle and women captives) • 6 Warrior Trophy Titles (Matuso, pp. 197–200, purified by tula mbaŋga 'breaking the peril' and celebrated in the kwaŋga victory parade wearing ukwalo skin finger-strips): (1) mutīætumo (slayer of a Maasai spearman), (2) mutīota (captor of a bow), (3) mutīoβīu (captor of a sword), (4) mutīaŋgua (captor of a garment), (5) mutīaþīaka (captor of a quiver), (6) mutīando (captor of a scabbard)

entries.english: Akamba Religion: Kīu vs. Þaīu, Aīmu Spirit Abodes, Mbæβo & Kīesu Exorcism, and Mulungu / Ngai / Mumbī / Mwatwaŋgī (Lindblom 1920 Ch. XIII, pp. 209–253)
entries.translation: Soul vs. Breath (pp. 209–211): kīu (shadow/soul that becomes an ancestral spirit aimu after death and reincarnates in grandchildren) vs. þaīu / mīæβa (physical breath/vitality; 'the heart is angry' = ŋgoo nī ndatū) • Ancestral Spirits (aīmu, sg. īīmu; cf. folktale ogre iīmu, pp. 210–228): dwell in sacred fig trees (mumo / kīumo) with sacrificial huts (kīlī / īþæmbo, Figs. 55–56) and on haunted mountains (Kyumbe, Kivauni, Muutha, Nengia, Nsambani, Kilui's pond); praying mantis = mwaŋgī wa aīmu / muŋgaīmu ('spirit's snuff-box'); sacrificial meal = īu īa aīmu • Foreign Spirit Possession (pp. 229–240): mbæβo / kīsulīa (Maasai, Galla, Swahili, or Kikuyu spirits possessing women, exorcised with maβuo / kīlumī drumming, Fig. 57–58) & the 1906–1908 kīesu convulsion dance triggered by European pith-helmets or fezzes • Supreme Being & Myths of Origin (pp. 243–253): Mulungu / Ngai, also called Mumbī ('The Creator/Potter') and Mwatwaŋgī ('The Cleaver' who shapes fingers and toes); Fig. 59 shows a medicine-man's calabash drawing of Ngai and Mulungu with wings; Creation myth of the first human pair emerging from a termite hole (muþumbini) and the second pair (mba-aīmu) cast down from the clouds onto Mt. Nzaui with footprints on the rock; Myth of Death (Chameleon vs. Weaver-bird/Thrush, pp. 252–253)

entries.english: Medicine-Men (Mundu Muə vs. Ītima vs. Mundu Mwoī), Kuausīa Divination, Uīīka Arch, Ŋgondu, Þaβu & Makwa (Lindblom 1920 Chs. XIV–XVI & Addenda, pp. 254–333, 576–578)
entries.translation: Practitioners (pp. 254–258, 300): mundu muə (diviner & ritual doctor called in dreams by ancestors) vs. ītima (herbalist/surgeon without divination) vs. mutumīa wa uku / mutumīa wa makwa (purification specialist) vs. mundu mwoī (practitioner of lethal black magic wuī / uoī) • Divination (kuausīa, Fig. 60, pp. 258–264): sounding the 1-stringed musical bow (uta) and shaking the calabash (kītītī) to cast pebbles/seeds (mbu) in odd numbers upon a leopard or hyrax skin • Amulets & Field Charms (pp. 270–290): muþæa (healing/magical powder), īþītu (amulet), kīþīao (protective ash/stone smear against crop thieves); wayside stone/twig-throwing custom = īþaβu (Addenda p. 576); burying an accidental-death arrow with closed eyes (p. 577) • Epidemic Scapegoat Arch (uīīka / mwītano, pp. 271–274): banana-stem arch through which the village & livestock pass to expel pestilence (mwīmu / kīaþī), transferring illness to a goat or woman driven across the border • Ritual Impurity (þaβu / makwa / uku, pp. 299–303) & Purificatory Emetic (ŋgondu, pp. 295–298): prepared from rock-hyrax (kīgondu / kīkīla) stomach contents and sedge roots • Snake-Charmers & Surgery (pp. 303–312): Kimia at Ikutha & Kivuvu imparting immunity (βīnīa) with scarification & burnt snake-head powder; excising swollen uvula (kalīmī) with a giraffe-hair loop and suturing wounds with acacia thorns (p. 312)

entries.english: Cosmology, Solar Observatory (Kīsūæsīo kīa Sīua), 4 Seasons & 11 Muutha vs. Machakos Months (Lindblom 1920 Ch. XVII, pp. 334–342)
entries.translation: Celestial Bodies (pp. 334–338, Fig. 63): sun = sīua, moon = mwæī, stars = ndata (thought to be campfires of the sky-beings aīsa), evening star (Venus) = ŋgæmandī ('wife of the moon'), morning star = kithioi ('second wife of the moon'), Pleiades = kīlīlī, Orion's Belt = nžælə, Milky Way = uta wa mbua ('rain-bow'), rainbow = uta wa ŋgai ('God's bow', linked to the horned rainbow-serpent mukūŋga-mbua on Mt. Mutitu, p. 274), comet = ndata īa kīsīþə ('star with a tail') / ndata īa īoa ('famine star'), quartz crystal = maβīa ma ndata ('star-stones'), solar eclipse = sīua nīþotə muþæa ('the sun is smeared with medicine') • Solar Observatory & Crinum Lily (pp. 338–339): kīsūæsīo kīa sīua (elder's sighting seat aligned with tree forks to track the solstice) & the blooming of the wild Crinum lily īla mwaka ('flower of the year') heralding the rains • 4 Seasons (p. 340): (1) mbua īa uwa (Oct.–Dec. lesser rains), (2) þano (Jan.–Feb. dry season), (3) mbua īandoa (Mar.–May greater rains), (4) nundu (June–Sept. cool cloudy dry season) • 11 Months in Muutha (East Ukamba) vs. Machakos (Ulu) (pp. 340–341): 1. mwą / kalą (planting), 2. wīmą (weeding), 3. umau / mwanza, 4. wa katano, 5. þandatu (first harvest), 6. mwonža, 7. nīanīa, 8. kænda, 9. īkumī, 10. muβīu (grass-burning), 11. oŋgonono (waiting for rain)

entries.english: Decorative Art, Dress, Ornaments, Tooth-Chipping (Nžæsa) & False Teeth, and Color Lexicon (Lindblom 1920 Chs. XX–XXI & Addenda, pp. 357–397, 580)
entries.translation: Calabash & Wood Carving (Ch. XX, pp. 357–370, Figs. 64–76): incised calabash bowls (kīkuu, nžælə) rubbed with soot (mbu) depicting hunting scenes, chameleons, tortoises, snakes, millipedes (ŋgoŋgo), stars & moons; wire-bound dance accessories (Figs. 74–75) and wire-inlaid elder stools (mumbə, Fig. 76) • Dress & Ornaments (Ch. XXI, pp. 371–389, Figs. 77–95): woman's greased skin dress = ua, girl's beaded leather tail = muþīta, girl's brass-cylinder apron = kīmcæŋgo (cylinders = nžalī), Conus shell collar disc = kīβuo, grass-root necklet = ndīwa, ivory armlet = kīlaa, beard/eyelash tweezers = ŋgosə (smaller) & ŋgola (elder's), aromatic powder perfume = kīutu (made from muutu, mukenea, muīwa, and sīlīli roots) • Body Pigments & Color Roots (pp. 389, 580): black = -īu (from soot mbu; also covers blue & green), white = -eu / nzau (from chalk/lime īea), red = -tunə (from red ochre clay ndo / nda; also covers yellow) • Cicatrization & Tooth-Chipping (pp. 390–396, Figs. 96–108): abdominal/arm scarification = ndemwa; tooth-chipping (kuseuβīa maīo) by specialist (mundu wa kuseuβīa maīo) using chisel (nžæsa) and wood block (muþīa) to file 4–8 upper incisors to sharp points, plus knocking out 2 lower incisors (kwīβa) and fitting hartebeest-bone false teeth fastened with fine iron wire (p. 395)!

entries.english: Musical Instruments (4 Drums, Mbæβə Fiddle, So Horn), Dances, Toys, River-Crossing Riddle & Kūīsī Mancala (Lindblom 1920 Chs. XXII–XXIII, pp. 398–428)
entries.translation: Musical Instruments (Ch. XXII, pp. 398–407, Figs. 109–114): (1) mbalīa / ŋguþa (long single-headed tubular dance drum, Fig. 109), (2) kīþæmbə (short cylinder drum played by women), (3) ŋgoma (double-headed drum in Kibwezi), (4) kīa / muβīŋgu (stamping tube drum beaten against the ground, Fig. 110); medicine-man's musical bow (Fig. 111); mbæβə (1-stringed bowed gourd fiddle, Fig. 112); so (bamboo/branch trumpet with calabash bell, Fig. 113); nžumalī (boy's reed flute, Fig. 114); metal leg-bells = īβamba • Dances (pp. 407–417, Figs. 115–116): mbalīa (somersault & drum dance led by bard ŋguī), musīa (unaccompanied song-dance), kīlamu (harvest youth dance), īβwulu (jumping dance on stilts in Kitui), kīlumī (women's spirit-possession dance) • Toys, Games & Counting-Out Rhyme (Ch. XXIII, pp. 418–428, Figs. 117–120): stalk & clay dolls (mwana, Figs. 117–118), spinning peg-top (ndīa, Fig. 119), plaited sling (kītuþya, Fig. 120), rolling-hoop target game (kwaþa ndīa), leopard-goat-sweet-potatoes river-crossing puzzle (p. 425), mancala board game (kūīsī, 2 rows of 8–20 holes played with mbu pebbles), and 10-word children's counting-out rhyme (p. 426): tali, talita, kaonda, mnaso, mbli, katumo, kēēti, muno, mnanda, mwitango ('one-eyed')

entries.english: Homestead Architecture (Musī / Kīeŋgo), Hut Interior (We / Kīβæta), Fire-Drilling & Domestic Etiquette (Lindblom 1920 Chs. XXIV–XXV, pp. 431–448)

XXIV, pp. 431–444, Figs. 121–126): homestead = musī (cattle post in wilderness = kīeŋgo); thorn hedge = wīio, narrow barricaded entrance = muβīa (closed with mīīŋgo bars), outside palaver yard with shade tree = þomə; conical thatched hut = nīumba (supported by central post kītsī and wall-poles ŋgītī); sleeping compartment = we (with parents' bed ututu and children's bed), kitchen/storage side = kīβæta, ceiling granary rack = īkumbī, miniature spirit-bed behind the 3 hearth-stones (maβīa ma īko) = kīīŋgə (for ancestral spirits aīmu, p. 439); grain storehouse on posts = īkumbī • Fire-Drilling (p. 440, Fig. 126): male twirling drill-stick = ulīndī (Cajanus indicus / mumbu fig), female flat hearth-board = kīka (forbidden to women) • Home Life & Taboos (Ch. XXV, pp. 445–448): firstwife = muka mukuu / kīβætī kīnænə; sweeping the hut at night or stepping over a person's legs is taboo; pointing direction is done by sticking out the tongue (p. 565); beckoning is done palm-downward (p. 565)

XXVI, pp. 449–464, Figs. 127–133): bow = uta (upper tip mbīa īa muþīa vs. lower butt mbīa īa ītīna; bowstring = uīa of back-sinew); feathered shaft = musīa (3 vulture feathers mbūī), foreshaft = uþunžī, removable iron head = mbalīo (wrapped in soft goatskin strip uβuha); wooden bird-arrows = īaŋgī (carved with blunt heads ndatī / nžæþo, Fig. 129); cylindrical leather quiver = þīaka (decked with ostrich-feather pompon kītuku, Fig. 130); sword = uβīu (in red leather scabbard ndo, Fig. 131); throwing clubs = ndata (wood Fig. 132 & stone-headed Fig. 133) • Arrow-Poison (muβaī / īβaī, pp. 454–457, Fig. 128): boiled from wood/roots of Acocanthera schimperi (mubaī tree) applied with spatula (kīβaīo) • Hunting & 7 Traps (Ch. XXVII, pp. 465–474, Figs. 134–138): elephant-hunting caravan leader = muthiani; bird-lime from boiled wild-fig sap = ulembwa (Addenda p. 579); traps: (1) kīambu (leopard/hyena box deadfall, Fig. 134), (2) mukwa (spring-pole running noose, Figs. 135–136), (3) īkæŋgə (baited trigger snare), (4) falling stone/slab bird trap (Fig. 137), (5) kītatī / kīsuŋgula (tubular spring mole-trap, Fig. 138), (6) spiked pitfall (īīma), (7) night-roost hand-catching at Machakos (p. 579)

entries.english: Hildegarde Hinde's (1904, pp. v–xviii, 2–75) Ulu (Machakos) vs. Nganyawa (Kitui) Dialect Comparison, 6 Plural Rules & Ku-tinda Verb Paradigm
entries.translation: Dialects & Phonology (pp. vi–viii): Ulu (Machakos to the coast) vs. Nganyawa (part of Kitui District, mutually intelligible with southern Kenya Province Akikuyu); Kamba lacks the letter r (except guttural rr), and b/v, g/k, and th/s/z interchange • 6 Plural Rules (pp. vi–vii): (1) mu- → a- (muka → aka 'woman', Mukamba → Akamba), (2) mu- → mi- (muti → miti 'tree'), (3) i- → ma- (ivia → mavia 'stone'), (4) ki- → i- (kiatu → iatu 'sandal', kibilla → ibilla 'chair' [Ulu] vs. kitumbi → itumbi [Nganyawa]), (5) invariable n- (nyumba → nyumba), (6) ka-/ki- → twa-/shi- (kana → twana/shiana 'child', kia → thia/sia 'finger/toe') • Complete Conjugation of Ku-tinda / Gu-tinda ('to conquer', pp. xii–xviii): Present Indefinite n-a-tinda, w-a-tinda, a-tinda, tw-a-tinda, mw-a-tinda, m-a-tinda; Present Imperfect ni-ki-tinda, wa/u-ki-tinda, a-ki-tinda, tu-ki-tinda, mu-ki-tinda, me/ma-ki-tinda; Present Perfect ni-tind-eti/-iti; Past Perfect ni-na-tind-ie (vs. Kikuyu ni-tind-eri); Future ni/nin-ka/ga-tinda (or conversational infinitive nin-ku-shoka 'I will return', p. xviii); Imperative tinda! (pl. tindani! / tindai!); Subjunctive ni-tinde; Negative Present n-di-tinda, wa/u-di/ndi-tinda...; Negative Past Perfect n-di-na-tinda; Negative Future n-di-ka/ga-tinda; Negative Imperative di/ndi-tinda! (pl. di/ndi-tindani! / tindai!); Negative Subjunctive n-di-tinde • Ceremonial dances, life stages & salutations (pp. 17, 65, 67, 72–75): kedume (elders' dance), wathi yaiitu (women's dance), mbaii (war-song); mweetu (girl/virgin), kibeti (married woman who has had 4 children), thāāta (barren woman), mkuu/kisee (old woman); Salutation (p. 75): o voo! — Reply: o voo nēza! / nēza!
entries.pronunciation: mu-ka-mba a-ka-mba / ni-na-tind-ie / ke-du-me / ki-be-ti / o voo ne-za

entries.english: Dr. Krapf's (1850, pp. vi–vii, 1–64) Kikámba Phonological Laws, Ivory Caravan Trade & "Kibo" Snow Entry
entries.translation: Wakamba Ethnography & Trade (pp. vi–vii): ~70,000–90,000 souls dwelling ~400 miles inland with colonies near the Rabbai Wanika, famous for carrying inland ivory (ino ya nzou) to Mombasa and preserving a tradition of southwestern origin • Two Kikámba Phonological Laws (p. vii): (1) total absence of the consonant R (regularly replaced by l or elided, e.g., ku-toma vs. Kinika ku-ruma), and (2) placement of the primary accent on the first radical syllable • Notable 1850 Kikámba Lexicon (pp. 1–64): Mulúngu (God, p. 23; aimu = ancestral spirits), kibo / mawía ma mbúa ("snow / Kibo [Kilimanjaro's snow dome]; stones of rain/hail", p. 46 — recording Rebmann & Krapf's 1848–1849 discovery of snow on Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya), mutumia (pl. atumia, elder/senator, p. 17), mundu mume (general/brave man, p. 22), mundu wa uoi / mundu wa muga (sorcerer vs. physician/diviner, pp. 37, 47), uvoo! (peace/salutation, p. 36), mbúka / ndéto (story/proverb, pp. 19, 39, 49)
